newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian president meets miners on leader's arrest.
newsitem.headline: Romanian president meets miners on leader's arrest.

text.p: Romania's centrist president met miners' leaders on Sunday but declined to intervene to release their trade union chief who is facing trial on charges connected to early post-communist violence.

Emil Constantinescu held talks at his Controceni palace with the miners' leaders from the country's main western Jiu Valley coalfields following trade union protests at the detention on Friday of union chief Miron Cosma.
The president, who invited reporters to attend the talks, said Cosma's detention was in order for the union chief to stand trial for his alleged role in the violence.

Constantinescu told the union leaders there should be no repeat of waves of violence when Cosma's miners beat up opposition protesters in 1990, followed by anti-reform riots during which the first post-communist government was toppled in 1991.
"This threat must disappear," the president said.

Constantinescu's centrists won last November's election -- ending the seven-year grip on power of ex-president Ion Iliescu's leftists -- pledging to bring to justice those responsible for that violence.

Police detained Cosma on Friday on a warrant accusing him of "undermining state authority" and breaking firearms regulations, charges which carry up to 15 years jail. A date for his trial should be set next week.

The charges are related to an episode in 1991, when Cosma led thousands of Jiu Valley coalminers on a three-day rampage in Bucharest, during which government offices were torched and three people were killed during clashes with security forces.
Jiu Valley union leaders ruled out a repeat of miner-led riots over Cosma's arrest, but they asked that their leader should get a fair trial.
"We don't want to see Cosma handcuffed and treated as a petty criminal," said Cosma's deputy Avram Virjeu. "The trial will bring to light many things that have been unknown so far."
Constantinescu declined to intervene to have Cosma released from police custody ahead of his trial.

"I will not allow that the criminal investigation should turn into one aimed against labour unions, or that it should acquire political connotations," he told the labour leaders who say they represent the 45,000 Jiu Valley pitmen.
Cosma was being investigated "as a citizen, not as a labour leader" for his role in the 1991 riots, during which former Prime Minister Petre Roman, a reformer, was forced to quit.
Roman, now head of the Senate, has blamed his downfall on a putsch engineered by communists around Iliescu.

Liberals have accused Iliescu of resorting to mob rule by summoning Cosma's miners to the capital to crush opposition protests. He has repeatedly denied those accusations, saying the riots had been "spontaneous".
